Painted redstart (Myioborus pictus) nestlings exhibit a predictable developmental sequence under the thermal conditions typical of their active metabolic periods. Upon emergence, chicks weigh roughly 1.36 grams [Wwb = roughly 1.36 grams], a remarkably low neonatal mass that underscores the altricial strategy of this species. This initial wet weight of 1.7 grams [Ww0 = 1.7 grams] represents the mass of the fertilised ovum at oviposition, reflecting the substantial yolk reserves allocated to the embryo. The considerable metabolic expenditure during development is reflected in the transition from egg to hatchling masses. Post-hatching, the parents commence intensive provisioning, and the nestlings begin a phase of rapid mass gain that will ultimately see them reach an adult body mass of 9.7 grams [Wwi = 9.7 grams]. This ultimate wet weight is consistent with values recorded for other small-bodied parulid warblers.

Under the elevated body temperatures characteristic of active foraging in this species, specifically 41.6 °C [T = 41.6 °C], several critical life-history milestones are achieved within a compressed timeframe. Fledging, the point at which the chick achieves sustained flight and departs the nest, occurs approximately 8 days after hatching [tx = approximately 8 days after hatching] at a temperature of 41.6 °C [T = 41.6 °C]. This rapid fledging period is likely an adaptation to reduce nest vulnerability to predation in the open pine-oak habitats the species occupies. Gonadal maturation, marking the onset of puberty, follows considerably later, with individuals reaching sexual maturity at about 24 days after hatching [tp = about 24 days after hatching] at a temperature of 41.6 °C [T = 41.6 °C]. This relatively fast pace of sexual maturation for a warbler allows young redstarts to potentially breed within their first season, a strategy facilitated by the abundant insect prey available during the monsoon period in their range.

The age at first successful reproduction, a key demographic parameter, is attained considerably later than puberty for Painted redstart. Field records from long-term banding studies in the Madrean Sky Islands indicate that individuals typically produce their first brood at around 292 days after birth [tR = around 292 days after birth], measured under the 41.6 °C [T = 41.6 °C] thermal environment of their active season. This substantial delay between reaching sexual maturity and actually initiating a first clutch is commonly observed in migratory passerines, reflecting the need to acquire a territory, secure a mate, and accumulate sufficient body condition for the energetic demands of egg production. The interval between hatching and first breeding is nearly twelve times the length of the fledging period, highlighting the prolonged juvenile phase necessary for developing foraging proficiency and social skills in this insectivorous warbler.

Reproductive output in Painted redstart is characterized by moderate fecundity and limited annual breeding attempts. Females typically produce a clutch of 3 to 4 eggs per nesting attempt [N_R_i = 3 to 4 eggs per nesting attempt], a typical value for parulids of this body size. Under favorable conditions, a pair may attempt 1 to 2 broods per season [F_R_i = 1 to 2 broods per season], yielding a maximum reproductive rate of approximately 3.7 offspring per year [Ri = approximately 3.7 offspring per year]. When maintained at an ambient temperature of 41.6 °C [T = 41.6 °C], the energetic demands of egg formation are considerable, and clutch size is often constrained by the availability of lepidopteran larvae during the critical early nestling period. This reproductive strategy, balancing moderate clutch size against the possibility of double-brooding, reflects the trade-offs inherent in breeding within a short montane summer window.

Longevity records for Painted redstart, derived from mist-netting and resighting data, indicate a maximum lifespan of approximately 6.6 years [am = approximately 6.6 years] under the 41.6 °C [T = 41.6 °C] thermal regime typical of its active foraging periods. This lifespan, while modest compared to some larger-bodied passerines, is respectable for a 9.7 gram warbler. Data from the constant-effort banding program in the Chiricahua Mountains suggest that annual adult survival is high, with many individuals returning to the same breeding territories across multiple seasons. The combination of a relatively extended lifespan and a low annual reproductive rate places this species along a slower pace-of-life continuum compared to temperate-breeding warblers. This survival strategy is adaptive in the unpredictable, monsoon-driven environment of its Sky Island habitat, where reproductive success in any single year may be highly variable.
